clue.text: Hairpiece in fashion again — it has hairpins in it

parts.note: a switch is a tress of false hair worn as a hairpiece
a style that is back is fashionable once more

explanation.surface: A wig that has come back into style is held in place with hairpins.
explanation.walkthrough: The hairpins are not for hair: they are hairpin bends, the tight turns of a zigzagging mountain road.
explanation.definitionFit: A zigzag mountain road climbs by tight hairpin bends, so hairpins are part of it.

clue.text: River erosion?

explanation.surface: Is the river eating away its banks?
explanation.definitionFit: One is a river through Durham in north-east England; the other is the gradual wasting of a surface by use or friction.

clue.text: Small bird steered with a handle

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
led means guided or steered

explanation.surface: A little bird is guided along by a handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A handle' is slang for a title such as Sir or Lady, so a person with a handle has a rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang calls a rank like Lord or Lady a handle to a name, so someone noble has one.

clue.text: Distemper for compact residence

explanation.surface: A paint for decorating a small, tidy flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distemper' reads as a wall paint; here it is the dog disease, one form of which hardens the pads of the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardpad is a form of canine distemper that toughens a dog's paws; a firm, compact pad is also slang for a home.

clue.text: A habit abroad

parts.note: a way is a custom or habit, as in 'set in one's ways'

explanation.surface: A custom picked up while travelling in foreign countries.
explanation.definitionFit: Being abroad means being out of the country, off somewhere else.

clue.text: Boy at university not finished with line of ship's timbers

indicators.note: the last letter of the university's name is cut off, so it is left unfinished

parts.note: Keele is a university in Staffordshire, England
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A lad who left his degree course unfinished goes off to the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: Keele is a campus university in Staffordshire; 'not finished' trims its last letter, and 'at' is just a link placing the boy alongside.
explanation.definitionFit: A keelson is the timber bolted along a ship's floor above the keel to stiffen it.

clue.text: Drawn outline of hotel suite refurbishment (10) 814p at this rate, for the sonnet?

indicators.note: a refurbishment rebuilds and rearranges a place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sketch showing a hotel suite after its makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refurbishment' rearranges HOTEL SUITE.
explanation.definitionFit: A silhouette is a dark shape drawn as an outline or profile against a light background.

clue.text: 14p at this rate, for the sonnet?

definitions.text: 14p at this rate, for the sonnet?

parts.words: 14p at this rate, for the sonnet?
parts.note: a sonnet has fourteen lines, so paying fourteen pence for one means paying a penny for each line, a phrase for cheap hack writing

explanation.surface: What a poet would earn if fourteen pence bought a whole sonnet.
explanation.walkthrough: A sonnet is a poem of fourteen lines; the phrase for that rate also describes poorly paid journalism.
explanation.definitionFit: Hack writers were once paid by the length of their copy, so the rate became a byword for cheap writing.

clue.text: Means of spearing fish

explanation.surface: A tool for spearing fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A pike is a long-shafted infantry spear; the pike is also a predatory freshwater fish.

clue.text: False trade-plate found in the Lake District

indicators.note: something false is not genuine, so the letters are rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A fake number plate turns up in the Lakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'False' rearranges TRADE-PLATE; a trade plate is a temporary number plate used by motor dealers.
explanation.definitionFit: Patterdale is a village at the head of Ullswater in Cumbria's Lake District.

clue.text: Plant growth will be found in relic, henceforth

indicators.note: says the answer lies in the run of letters across the next words

explanation.surface: Some moss will grow on the old relic from now on.
explanation.definitionFit: Lichen is a slow-spreading growth of fungus and alga on rocks and bark, loosely counted as a plant.

clue.text: Fowler, say, a would-be flier?

explanation.surface: A bird-catcher who dreams of taking to the air himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A fowler catches birds, as does a bird-catcher; a person who tries to fly with strapped-on wings was also so called.

clue.text: Backer has been upset by agent

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of been are rearranged

parts.note: a factor is an agent who acts for another, as for a landowner

explanation.surface: A financial supporter is put out by a middleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backer' means a sponsor, not something behind; 'upset' gives BENE from the three words' middle one, and 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefactor gives money or help, just as a backer supports a venture.

clue.text: Back garden, perhaps, given a new look

parts.note: the rear is the back

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of garden might be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: The back garden has been relandscaped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back garden' reads as one place, but 'Back' is its own piece and 'perhaps' turns garden into RANGED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something laid out afresh in a different order has been altered in its appearance.

clue.text: Bottle never broken

indicators.note: broken means smashed into bits, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A bottle that has never been smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is British slang for courage.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, bottle is courage, the same as daring or pluck.

clue.text: Method used when in favour of loose maul

parts.note: being for something means supporting it

indicators.note: loose means set free and untidy, so the letters of maul are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rugby tactic used when backing a loose maul.
explanation.walkthrough: A maul in rugby is a scrum-like tussle around the ball carrier; 'loose' turns it into MULA.
explanation.definitionFit: A formula is a set method or recipe for doing something.

clue.text: Nothing in the clenched fingers to pass off

indicators.note: the letter for nothing goes inside the word for clenched fingers

parts.note: a fist is a hand with the fingers clenched
O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: An empty fist used to fob someone off.
explanation.definitionFit: To foist something is to palm it off fraudulently as genuine.

clue.text: Little Maureen's in the den, little devil

indicators.note: the short name goes inside the word for den

parts.note: taken as written
Mo is a short form of Maureen

explanation.surface: Little Maureen is in the den, the little imp.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's means 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A demon is an evil spirit, and a mischievous child is called a little devil.

clue.text: Cowpat?

parts.note: split into two words: an old word for a cow or ox, and pat meaning exactly or tidily

explanation.surface: A dropping in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the clue word: an archaic word for cattle (as in neatsfoot oil) plus pat, meaning exactly or tidily.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant cattle and today means tidy or exactly right, as pat does.

clue.text: Needle-case found in the Tuileries

indicators.note: says the answer sits within the letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A sewing kit picked up in the Paris gardens.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tuileries is a famous garden in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles and sewing items.

clue.text: A great stop at sea

parts.note: vast means huge or great

explanation.surface: A big stop made while sailing.
explanation.definitionFit: Avast is a sailor's command to halt or cease.

clue.text: One may even the score of England's openers in grave trouble

indicators.note: trouble here stirs things up, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: the opening two letters of England

explanation.surface: A cricketer who may level the match after England's openers struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'England's openers' gives EN, the first two letters; 'trouble' mixes these with GRAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenger takes revenge, settling a score with a wrongdoer.

clue.text: In "The Grapes of Wrath", did he have a walking-on part?

definitions.text: In "The Grapes of Wrath", did he have a walking-on part?

parts.words: In "The Grapes of Wrath", did he have a walking-on part?
parts.note: the Battle Hymn of the Republic says 'He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored', so the person in that line crushes grapes underfoot

explanation.surface: A question about a bit part in a famous novel or film.
explanation.walkthrough: A walk-on part is a tiny acting role, but here it means someone who walks on grapes to press them.
explanation.definitionFit: One who treads grapes walks on them to crush out the juice.

clue.text: Exotic fruit and vegetable starters under the table, we hear

indicators.note: exotic means strange and foreign, so these letters are made unfamiliar

parts.note: the opening two letters of the word vegetable

explanation.surface: Unusual produce for an appetiser, slipped secretly beneath the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exotic' turns the fruit into FURTI; 'vegetable starters' are its opening pair. The trailing 'we hear' has no evident job and may be stray text.
explanation.definitionFit: Underhand, secret dealings are done under the table, as a furtive person acts.

clue.text: Vessel once controlled by three big banks?

definitions.text: Vessel once controlled by three big banks?

parts.words: Vessel once controlled by three big banks?
parts.note: the banks are tiers of oarsmen, not lending firms, rowing an ancient warship

explanation.surface: A ship owned by a consortium of three major lenders.
explanation.walkthrough: A bank here is a tier of oars; the ancient Greek warship had three.
explanation.definitionFit: A trireme was an ancient galley rowed by oarsmen sitting in three tiers.

clue.text: Ways to go to find one's origins, we hear

indicators.note: says the word is identified by how it is spoken

parts.note: a person's roots are their origins

explanation.surface: Paths to follow in search of your ancestry.
explanation.definitionFit: Routes are paths or courses taken to reach a place.

clue.text: Tin, there, in the gorge?

parts.note: a can is a tin
yon is an old word for over there

explanation.surface: Is there tin to be found in the ravine?
explanation.definitionFit: A canyon is a deep, steep-sided ravine, a large gorge.

clue.text: Motorway, very loud, leads to pretty quarrel

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, read as letters MI
ff, fortissimo, is the musical mark for very loud

explanation.surface: Noise from the motorway sparks a neighbourly row.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is a motorway from London to Leeds, its 1 read as an I.
explanation.definitionFit: A miff is a minor tiff or fit of pique.

clue.text: Stake in Dante's work

indicators.note: says the answer lies within the letters of the poet's name

explanation.surface: A bet placed on the Divine Comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: An ante is the stake put into the pot before a poker hand.

clue.text: Piece for sharpening stringendo playing?

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are performed freely in a new order

explanation.surface: A passage of music marked to speed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Stringendo is a musical direction meaning gradually faster; 'playing' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A grindstone is a revolving stone wheel used for sharpening blades.

clue.text: University in which none are gated

explanation.surface: A college where no student is ever confined.
explanation.walkthrough: Being gated is being confined to college as a punishment, which a university with no residents never does.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's distance-learning university admits all comers; the adjective also means unbarred, with no gate shut.

clue.text: Arden, for example, surrounded by hard grass must be planted anew

indicators.note: the second word wraps around the first, enclosing it

parts.note: a reed is a tall, stiff grass
Arden is a forest in Warwickshire, setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: The Forest of Arden, ringed by tough grass, must be replanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Reforested land has had trees put back in it again.
